items.prompt: Identify two distinct indicators useful for comparing economic development beyond total money output.
items.canonical_answer: Real income per person and access to education or health services provide distinct information.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): real per-capita measure. Distinct characteristic/example (1): service access.

items.prompt: Explain how reliable transport and relevant training can support development where equipment is currently underused through delays and missing skills.
items.canonical_answer: Transport eases input and market access, while training enables workers to use equipment effectively. More usable output can be produced from available resources; wider living-standard gains depend on per-capita outcomes, distribution and environmental conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): transport/training improved. Mechanism (2): fewer delays (1), relevant productive skills (1). Consequence (1): capacity used more effectively with welfare conditions.

items.prompt: Define a developed economy using more than a sector label.
items.canonical_answer: An economy generally combining relatively high real income per person with broad productive capacity and access to services.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): high real per-capita income with broader capacity/service development.

items.prompt: Identify two qualifications to the inference that high national average income means every household has good living conditions.
items.canonical_answer: Income can be unequally distributed and service access can vary by region or household.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): distribution. Distinction/example (1): access variation.

items.prompt: Define a developing economy without assuming all such economies are identical.
items.canonical_answer: An economy improving productive capacity and living conditions while often facing lower average incomes or more limited access to services.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): developing capacity/conditions with relevant constraints, not a uniform stereotype.

items.prompt: Identify two complementary constraints in an invented developing economy where a machine is available but workers lack relevant skills and roads delay input deliveries.
items.canonical_answer: Missing relevant training and unreliable transport limit effective use of the machine.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): skills. Distinct characteristic/example (1): transport.

items.prompt: Evaluate an invented processing project that creates jobs and usable output but increases pollution and housing pressure; its funding is affordable and controls are feasible but require resources.
items.canonical_answer: Jobs and value added can support development, but pollution and housing pressure impose costs and gains may be uneven. Conditional support depends on useful output, fair access, effective environmental controls and service capacity, rather than output growth alone.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): jobs (1), usable output (1). Argument against (2): pollution (1), housing/distribution pressure (1). Condition (1): controls and complementary services. Judgement (2): conditional support (1), connected to net per-capita/distribution/environmental outcomes (1). Total 7.

items.prompt: Explain total population change for an invented initial population 10,000 with annual births 300, deaths 100, immigration 80 and emigration 120.
items.canonical_answer: Natural increase is 200; net migration is −40. Total change is 160, giving final population 10,160 and a 1.6% increase using the stated initial base.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): births/deaths and movement. Mechanism (2): natural +200 (1), migration −40 (1). Consequence (1): total +160, distinct from natural change.

items.prompt: Explain why equal total population growth rates do not establish equal demographic causes in two countries.
items.canonical_answer: One may have large natural increase offset by emigration, while another gains through net immigration. Births, deaths and migration must be examined separately.
marking_guidance: Context (1): same total, possible different flows. Reason/conclusion (1): distinguish natural change and net migration.

items.prompt: Explain the error in reporting total population increase as births minus deaths when net migration is negative 40.
items.canonical_answer: Births minus deaths gives natural increase. Total change must also subtract the net outflow of 40, so the natural and total figures differ.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): natural change treated as total. Boundary/test (1): include net migration −40.

items.prompt: Define the crude birth rate.
items.canonical_answer: Live births per thousand people over a stated period, usually a year.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Live births per thousand people over a stated period, usually a year.

items.prompt: Identify the numerator and denominator for a crude birth rate.
items.canonical_answer: Annual live births and the specified whole population.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested component or influence. Distinction/example (1): second component or correct interpretation with stated period.

items.prompt: Define the crude death rate.
items.canonical_answer: Deaths per thousand people over a stated period, usually a year.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Deaths per thousand people over a stated period, usually a year.

items.prompt: Identify two influences that prevent a crude death rate alone being a complete health-service ranking.
items.canonical_answer: Age structure and health conditions can both affect the crude rate.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested component or influence. Distinction/example (1): second component or correct interpretation with stated period.

items.prompt: Define a fertility rate.
items.canonical_answer: A measure of births relative to women, with the general annual rate distinguished from the expected lifetime total fertility rate.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): A measure of births relative to women, with the general annual rate distinguished from the expected lifetime total fertility rate.

items.prompt: Identify the interpretation and time horizon of a stated total fertility rate of 2.5.
items.canonical_answer: It summarises estimated lifetime births per woman under the period’s age-specific rates, not 2.5 births each year.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested component or influence. Distinction/example (1): second component or correct interpretation with stated period.

items.prompt: Define net migration.
items.canonical_answer: Immigration minus emigration over the stated period.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Immigration minus emigration over the stated period.

items.prompt: Identify immigration, emigration and the net result for an invented area with 80 arrivals and 120 departures.
items.canonical_answer: Immigration 80, emigration 120; net migration −40.
marking_guidance: Feature/characteristic (1): first requested component or influence. Distinction/example (1): second component or correct interpretation with stated period.

items.prompt: Explain how a larger working-age cohort can support production when relevant skills, jobs, equipment and services are available.
items.canonical_answer: More people can enter productive work and use complementary resources to expand real output and earnings. The gain requires jobs and capacity; per-capita output, distribution and environmental effects still condition living-standard conclusions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): working-age cohort larger. Mechanism (2): jobs use skills (1), equipment/services support output (1). Consequence (1): conditional productive potential, not guaranteed welfare.

items.prompt: Explain why 600 working-age residents are not the same as 600 employed workers when only 300 have jobs.
items.canonical_answer: Working age is a demographic category. Employment depends on actual work, so an age-based dependency ratio does not measure the number earning employment income.
marking_guidance: Context (1): 600 age group versus 300 jobs. Reason/conclusion (1): structure differs from actual employment.

items.prompt: Define net migration (2). Identify two development indicators (2). Explain how unchanged births with fewer deaths can raise natural population increase (2). Identify the terms for live births per thousand people annually and deaths per thousand people annually (2).
items.canonical_answer: Net migration is immigration minus emigration over a period. Real income per person and service access are indicators. Fewer deaths widen births minus deaths when births are unchanged; total change also includes migration. The definitions identify crude birth and death rates.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): immigration less emigration (1), stated period (1). Separate points for indicators (2): real income per person (1), service access (1). Explanation (2): deaths fall (1), natural difference widens with births unchanged (1). Identification (2): birth rate (1), death rate (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented developing district: equipment exists but transport is unreliable and training access limited. Initial population 10,000; births 300, deaths 100, immigration 80 and emigration 120 in one year. Better service access is planned. A large group will enter working age; some genuine vacancies exist, but housing and school capacity are limited. All numbers use the same area and period. Describe three development/population features with a detail each (6). Explain how the development constraints and demographic flows affect productive capacity and population change (7). Discuss the opportunities and pressures from the larger working-age group during development (7).
items.canonical_answer: Transport and training constrain equipment use; natural increase is 200; net migration is −40. Removing delays and building skills can improve capacity. Natural increase plus net migration gives +160 and final 10,160. A larger workforce can fill jobs and raise output where skills/equipment fit, but limited housing and services and insufficient jobs can restrict benefits. Conditional gains require complementary investment and attention to per-capita outcomes, distribution and environment.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): capacity constraint (1), transport/training detail (1); natural increase (1), 200 detail (1); net migration (1), −40 detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): transport reduces delays (1), training improves use (1), both complement equipment (1); births less deaths 200 (1), migration −40 (1), total +160 (1), final 10,160 (1). Both sides/judgement (7): potential labour/output (1), genuine jobs opportunity (1); housing pressure (1), service/skill constraint (1); condition jobs and complementary capacity (1); judgement conditional development gain (1), tied to per-capita/distribution/environmental outcomes (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

facts: Invented developing district: equipment exists but transport is unreliable and training access limited. Initial population 10,000; births 300, deaths 100, immigration 80 and emigration 120 in one year. Better service access is planned. A large group will enter working age; some genuine vacancies exist, but housing and school capacity are limited. All numbers use the same area and period.

items.prompt: Invented equal-sized cohorts enter working age in two developing districts. Case 1 has relevant training, genuine jobs, usable equipment and expanding housing/services; pollution controls have a funded plan. Case 2 lacks enough jobs and training, housing/services are already strained and environmental controls are weak. No current national demographic statistic is implied. Evaluate the development opportunity in Case 1 (7). Evaluate the same cohort increase in Case 2 (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: productive work can raise output and earnings, while services support use of the workforce. Adjustment and environmental costs remain, so benefit is conditional on effective delivery and distribution. Case 2: the larger potential workforce may remain unused, with unemployment and pressure on facilities; future gains require jobs, skills and services. Equal cohort size does not produce equal development outcomes.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for labour/output (1), earnings and services (1); argument against adjustment cost (1), environmental/distribution risk (1); condition effective funded complements (1); judgement opportunity supported (1), tied to actual productive use (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for future potential (1), larger possible market/workforce (1); argument against insufficient jobs (1), service/environment pressure (1); condition complements must improve (1); judgement immediate gains limited (1), equal size not equal outcome (1). Total 14.
